title: Can people really die of fright?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether people can die of fright. They open with Jerry's near-death scares and a brief overview of fight-or-flight and adrenaline. They discuss sudden death, neurocardiology and Dr. Martin Samuels's work on contraction bands in the heart, plus the Baskerville Effect named after Conan Doyle's Hound of the Baskervilles. They cover a study of unlucky-fourth-of-the-month deaths in China and Japan, the 1994 Northridge earthquake spike in sudden deaths, and Walter Cannon's 1942 voodoo death paper. They debunk the idea that fear turns hair white overnight, and close with listener mail corrections (Diving Bell and Butterfly, hypoallergenic cats as a breed not a species, yeast as a fungus).

segments.title: Opening banter and Jerry's near-death scares
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, recounting producer Jerry's frightening experiences, including an elevator drop in Atlanta. They give a brief overview of fight-or-flight and adrenaline and introduce the idea of sudden death.

segments.title: Sudden death and neurocardiology
segments.summary: They define sudden death and discuss neurocardiology and Dr. Martin Samuels, who studies the link between fear and the heart. Because animal and experimental testing is unethical, he relies on anecdotal evidence from hearts of people who died suddenly. He found contraction bands, red stripes of heart lesions caused by adrenaline, which also appear in cocaine users.

segments.title: Contraction bands and the Baskerville Effect
segments.summary: They discuss how contraction bands grow more severe the longer time passes between an accident and death, and how adrenaline links to them. They introduce the Baskerville Effect, named after the heart attack in Conan Doyle's The Hound of the Baskervilles.

segments.title: Unlucky fourth of the month in China and Japan
segments.summary: A study of death certificates in China and Japan found higher mortality on the fourth of the month, since the number four sounds like the word for death. Those with heart disease, especially hospitalized patients, showed increased deaths compared with a white control group.

segments.title: Northridge earthquake sudden death spike
segments.summary: On the day of the Northridge earthquake, Los Angeles saw twenty-four sudden deaths, against a normal of about five. Most were attributed to fright rather than physical exertion, though the victims were on the older side and few had prior heart disease.

segments.title: Voodoo death and Walter Cannon
segments.summary: They describe Walter Cannon's 1942 paper arguing that sudden death was more common where voodoo was practiced, and that belief in being hexed could lead people to die. Cannon, a Harvard physiologist, is credited with starting the modern study of sudden death.

segments.title: Fear and hair turning white
segments.summary: They debunk the idea that hair can turn white overnight from fear. Stress may affect hair color through metabolic change, but not overnight. Sudden graying-looking hair loss comes from alopecia areata, and dead hair cells cannot change color.

segments.title: Listener mail and corrections
segments.summary: Corrections cover the Diving Bell and Butterfly memoir, which was blinked letter by letter to a transcriber rather than typed on a computer. Also covered are hypoallergenic cats, which are a new breed rather than a new species, and yeast, which is a fungus.

segments.title: Sign-off and related articles
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the Molly Edmonds article this episode is based on, the stuff Mom Never Told You podcast, and related Friday the 13th and urban legend content on the website.
